hints: Start by comparing where oxygen is more concentrated - the air in the alveolus or the blood arriving at the lungs - and remember what type of passive movement this sets up.
Think about the exact barriers oxygen must cross to get from alveolar air to blood plasma, focusing on how thin the cells are.
Finish the journey into the red blood cell and consider what happens to the oxygen concentration in plasma as oxygen keeps leaving it, keeping the gradient going.
walkthrough:
Set Up The Gradient**
Fresh air in the alveolus has a high partial pressure of oxygen, while deoxygenated blood arriving at the lung capillary has a lower partial pressure. That difference means there is a steep diffusion gradient from alveolus to blood, so net movement is passive and needs no energy.

Cross The Exchange Surface**
The pathway is kept very short for fast diffusion. Oxygen crosses the thin squamous cells of the alveolar wall, then a tiny gap of connective tissue, then the thin endothelial cells of the capillary wall to reach the blood plasma. Both walls are only one cell thick.

Enter Red Blood Cells**
From plasma, oxygen diffuses through the cell surface membrane of red blood cells. As oxygen binds to haemoglobin inside the cells, the dissolved oxygen concentration in plasma stays low, so the gradient from alveolus to blood is maintained and diffusion continues.

Final answer: Oxygen moves by diffusion down a concentration / partial pressure gradient from alveolus to blood. It diffuses across the squamous epithelium of the alveolar wall and the endothelium of the capillary wall into the plasma, then into red blood cells.

hints: Read horizontally from 2.7 kPa and 13.0 kPa up to the curve, then across to the y-axis to get two percentage saturation values before subtracting.
walkthrough:
Read And Subtract**
Find $2.7 \text{ kPa}$ on the x-axis, go up to the curve and across - you get about $34-36\%$. Do the same at $13.0 \text{ kPa}$ - you get about $97-98\%$. Subtract: about $97 - 35 = 62$. Always show both readings in your working and give the answer as % or percentage points.
Final answer: At $2.7 \text{ kPa} \approx 35\%$ saturation; at $13.0 \text{ kPa} \approx 97\%$ saturation; difference $= 97 - 35 = \approx 62$ percentage points.

hints: Think about what high partial pressure in the lungs should do to haemoglobin if it is to pick up as much oxygen as possible.
Now think about the opposite end - respiring tissues with low partial pressure - and what haemoglobin must do there to be useful.
Link this loading and unloading cycle to why cells need a constant oxygen delivery, using data from Fig. 4.1 to support your point.
walkthrough:
Load Where Oxygen Is Plentiful**
In the lungs the partial pressure is high. Haemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen there, so oxygen binds readily and oxyhaemoglobin is formed. Fig. 4.1 shows this as near 100% saturation above about $10-13 \text{ kPa}$, so almost every haemoglobin molecule is fully loaded.

Unload Where Oxygen Is Scarce**
In actively respiring tissues the partial pressure is low, around $2-4 \text{ kPa}$. There haemoglobin has a low affinity, so oxyhaemoglobin dissociates and oxygen is released. Fig. 4.1 shows saturation falls steeply to about $35\%$ at $2.7 \text{ kPa}$, meaning about $60\%$ of the carried oxygen has been given up.

Why This Matters**
That big difference between loading and unloading is the advantage. A small drop in partial pressure causes a large drop in saturation, so a lot of oxygen is delivered exactly where it is needed for aerobic respiration in cells, while loading in the lungs stays maximal.

Final answer: At high $pO_2$ in lungs haemoglobin has high affinity and loads oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin, e.g. ~97% saturated at 13.0 kPa. At low $pO_2$ in tissues affinity is low so oxyhaemoglobin dissociates and releases oxygen, e.g. only ~35% saturated at 2.7 kPa. This allows large uptake in lungs and large release to tissues for aerobic respiration.

hints: Start from the idea of normal body function and health, then think about what must go wrong for us to call something a disease.
To add the second mark, think about how that abnormal change shows itself or affects the person, for example in signs, symptoms or reduced effectiveness.
walkthrough:
Abnormal Function**
A healthy body carries out its normal processes effectively. A disease is when there is an abnormal change that stops the body working normally - it is the opposite of good health.

Visible Effect**
That change is not just invisible. It produces an adverse effect such as specific signs and symptoms, or a loss of physical, mental and social well-being. It can be infectious or non-infectious, like sickle cell anaemia.

Final answer: A disease is an abnormal change / condition in the body that prevents normal functioning / absence of good health. It has an adverse effect, producing specific signs and symptoms / reducing physical, mental or social well-being.

hints: Recall what type of gene mutation causes sickle cell anaemia and which gene it affects, without yet naming the amino acid.
Follow the flow of protein synthesis - how does a changed DNA triplet affect mRNA and then the amino acid brought by tRNA?
Think about which level of protein structure is changed first when one amino acid in the chain is different.
Consider how that single change alters the overall 3D shape and properties of the haemoglobin molecule, especially its solubility.
For full detail, recall the exact sixth codon change and the chemical nature of glutamic acid versus valine.
walkthrough:
The Gene Change**
The normal allele $Hb^A$ and sickle allele $Hb^S$ differ by a single base substitution in the gene coding for the beta-globin polypeptide. Only one triplet is altered, but that is enough to change the protein.

From Codon To Amino Acid**
Transcription produces a different mRNA codon. At the ribosome a different tRNA brings a different amino acid. So the primary structure - the sequence of amino acids - is altered.

Change In Shape**
That one different side chain changes how the polypeptide folds and how the four subunits pack together. Both tertiary and quaternary structure are changed. Glutamic acid is polar and hydrophilic, while valine is non-polar and hydrophobic, and it sits on the exterior of the molecule.

Change In Behaviour**
Because of the exposed non-polar patch, deoxygenated sickle haemoglobin is much less soluble. Molecules stick together and form long fibres inside the red blood cell, distorting it into a sickle shape and making it less able to bind and transport oxygen.

Precise Detail For Top Marks**
Quote the classic example: the sixth codon changes from GAG to GUG in mRNA (GTG instead of GAG in the non-template DNA strand, CAC instead of CTC in the template strand). The sixth amino acid is therefore valine instead of glutamic acid.

Final answer: HbS differs by a base substitution in the beta-globin gene. Altered mRNA codon causes a different amino acid in the primary structure: valine instead of glutamic acid at position 6 (GAG to GUG in mRNA, GAG to GTG in non-template DNA). This changes tertiary / quaternary structure, making haemoglobin less soluble so molecules stick together to form fibres and bind oxygen less well.
